title: Reconstructing hidden observables via quantum snapshot thermometry

paper.title: Reconstructing hidden observables via quantum snapshot thermometry
paper.abstract:
Abstract Projective snapshots are a standard readout tool for quantum simulators, but they directly probe only observables that are diagonal in the measurement basis.
We show how local equilibration and an independently calibrated equilibrium equation of state can reveal otherwise hidden conserved-density profiles. We demonstrate numerically that such “quantum snapshot thermometry” can recover energy fronts and a diffusion constant, distinguish spin transport from energy spreading, and reveal conserved-charge profiles invisible in the initial measurements.
We also identify symmetry-imposed ambiguities in the readout and show how prior knowledge of the spatial structure can resolve them.
Fixed-basis snapshot thermometry thus provides quantitative hydrodynamic information beyond transport exponents, bypassing additional measurement bases and quantum state tomography.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: In analog quantum simulators, key information about the many-body wave function is extracted from site-resolved projective measurements [ 1 , 2 , 68 , 27 , 16 ] . These wave-function snapshots give direct access to observables that are diagonal in the measurement basis. However, many quantities of interest, such as local energy, contain off-diagonal terms and thus cannot be directly determined from the snapshots. Such observables can be accessed through additional measurement settings, including basis rotations and randomized measurement protocols [ 23 , 18 ] , which can be challenging on platforms with limited coherent control [ 40 ] . Alternatively, off-diagonal observables can be inferred from fixed-basis measurements following known Hamiltonian dynamics [ 22 , 40 , 51 ] , although reconstructing them can require computationally expensive processing in an exponentially large Hilbert space. Hamiltonian shadow protocols alleviate this cost by using independently evolving patches [ 40 ] , while other protocols employ ancillary degrees of freedom [ 61 , 44 ] . These approaches use dedicated quantum dynamics to encode information into measurement outcomes, motivating a complementary strategy that exploits local equilibration during the dynamics of interest. Recent work has proposed that principal component analysis (PCA) of wave-function snapshots can diagnose transport and extract the associated dynamical exponents [ 4 , 70 ] . The observed correspondence between PCA entropy and energy transport raises the question of how a conserved-density profile becomes encoded in snapshot statistics when the corresponding operator is not diagonal in the measurement basis. Understanding this mechanism could enable quantitative reconstruction of the evolving profile, including its amplitude and shape, beyond transport exponents. A possible route is suggested by equilibrium thermometry, where equations of state and fluctuation relations connect measurable observables to thermodynamic quantities [ 47 , 36 , 20 , 50 ] . Atom-resolved fluctuation measurements have also enabled local thermometry without requiring global thermal equilibrium [ 13 ] . Here we show that local equilibration enables quantitative reconstruction of hidden conserved-density profiles from fixed-basis snapshots, without additional measurement operations or global dynamical reconstruction. Once local equilibration is established, an independently calibrated equilibrium equation of state (EOS) relates measurable diagonal observables to the local conserved densities. Where this relation is locally invertible, it converts snapshot averages into the density profile [Fig. 1 (a)]. Note that global invertibility is not essential: independent information about the preparation and spatial structure of the evolving profile can select the appropriate EOS branch. We demonstrate that this readout recovers the shape and amplitude of energy fronts and enables extraction of the diffusion constant. With multiple conserved quantities, different observables extracted from the same snapshots distinguish their transport responses, e.g., spin transport from energy spreading [Fig. 1 (b)]. The framework also applies beyond energy-conserving dynamics, enabling reconstruction of conserved-charge profiles in Floquet circuits that are not directly accessible in the measurement basis. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the local-equilibrium readout, its requirements and sources of error. Sections III - V apply this approach to numerically demonstrate energy reconstruction in the mixed-field Ising model, joint spin and energy readout in the XXZ chain, and hidden conserved-charge reconstruction in a Floquet circuit, respectively. Section VI examines symmetry-imposed ambiguities and branch-resolved reconstruction on the example of blockaded Rydberg atom arrays. Section VII explains the relation of PCA entropy [ 4 , 70 ] with local spin variance and identifies conditions under which it inherits transport scaling. Our conclusions are presented in Section VIII , while the appendices provide supporting analytical and numerical details.

sections.heading: II Local equilibration and readout
sections.text: Let 𝒒 ⁡ ( x , t ) ≡ { q a ​ ( x , t ) } \bm{q}(x,t)\equiv\{q_{a}(x,t)\} denote a set of local conserved densities, while 𝑶 ⁡ ( x , t ) ≡ { O a ​ ( x , t ) } \bm{O}(x,t)\equiv\{O_{a}(x,t)\} are the diagonal observables accessible from snapshots. Local equilibration relates these observables to the conserved densities through an equilibrium equation of state (EOS) [ 54 ] : O a ​ ( x , t ) = O a , eq ​ [ 𝒒 ⁡ ( x , t ) ] + r a ​ ( x , t ) , O_{a}(x,t)=O_{a,\mathrm{eq}}[\bm{q}(x,t)]+r_{a}(x,t), (1) where r a r_{a} denotes departures from the chosen equilibrium relation, including the influence of possible degrees of freedom beyond 𝒒 \bm{q} . For the example in Fig. 1 (a) with a single conserved density, r a r_{a} is the vertical displacement from the equilibrium curve at a given density q q , and the orange arrow depicts the process of local relaxation toward this curve. Once r a r_{a} becomes small, the measured average O meas O_{\rm meas} gives the reconstructed density q snap = O eq − 1 ​ ( O meas ) , q_{\rm snap}=O_{\rm eq}^{-1}(O_{\rm meas}), (2) on a selected invertible EOS branch. This forms the basis of our thermometry protocol, illustrated by dashed arrows in Fig. 1 (a). The described protocol requires knowledge of 𝑶 eq ​ ( 𝒒 ) \bm{O}_{\rm eq}(\bm{q}) , which should be obtained via an independent calibration. We do this by evaluating the diagonal observables and conserved densities in uniform equilibrium states spanning the relevant density range. In this work, we will focus on one-dimensional (1D) systems and finite-temperature regimes, where local equilibrium averages can be evaluated efficiently using thermal matrix product state (MPS) methods, with the system size needed for calibration set by convergence of the local observables. However, the thermometry protocol itself is not dimension-specific. In higher dimensions, the EOS could be obtained using other numerical methods or experimental measurements, provided that they associate observable values with independently determined conserved densities. At fixed system parameters, the same EOS can be reused for different preparations whenever the evolving observables follow the calibrated relation. For small deviations from a uniform reference density 𝒒 0 \bm{q}_{0} , the linear response is governed by the EOS Jacobian 𝒥 a ​ α ​ ( 𝒒 ) = ∂ O a , eq ​ ( 𝒒 ) ∂ q α , \mathcal{J}_{a\alpha}(\bm{q})=\frac{\partial O_{a,\mathrm{eq}}(\bm{q})}{\partial q_{\alpha}}, (3) evaluated at 𝒒 = 𝒒 0 \bm{q}=\bm{q}_{0} . For a single conserved quantity, a nonzero EOS slope allows readout from one diagonal observable. For energy readout, this derivative also characterizes the observable’s leading coupling to the slow energy mode, connecting the EOS response to hydrodynamic relaxation [ 8 , 67 ] . With several conserved quantities, each observable generally mixes their contributions. Resolving all densities q a q_{a} at linear order requires 𝒥 \mathcal{J} to have full column rank, so that the observables respond independently to changes in the densities. For equal numbers of observables and densities, this condition reduces to det 𝒥 ≠ 0 \det\mathcal{J}\neq 0 . Furthermore, when linearization about 𝒒 0 \bm{q}_{0} is insufficient, reconstruction should use the full EOS. Figure 1 (b) illustrates the general protocol with multiple hidden conserved densities q a q_{a} reconstructed from diagonal observables O a O_{a} , measured in the same ensemble of snapshots. A typical example is the joint readout of spin and energy: while magnetization m m is diagonal in the standard Pauli basis, energy e e contains off-diagonal terms that ordinarily require additional measurement settings to access. The same snapshot ensemble provides the local magnetization m i = ⟨ σ ^ i z ⟩ m_{i}=\langle\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{z}\rangle and nearest-neighbor correlation C i = ⟨ σ ^ i z ​ σ ^ i + 1 z ⟩ C_{i}=\langle\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{z}\hat{\sigma}_{i+1}^{z}\rangle . In the notation above, these correspond to 𝒒 = ( m , e ) \bm{q}=(m,e) and 𝑶 = ( m , C ) \bm{O}=(m,C) . Magnetization gives the spin density m ⁡ ( x , t ) m(x,t) directly. The independently calibrated relation C = C eq ​ ( e , m ) C=C_{\rm eq}(e,m) then determines the energy e ⁡ ( x , t ) e(x,t) from the measured magnetization, provided that ∂ e C eq ≠ 0 \partial_{e}C_{\rm eq}\neq 0 . A few comments are in order. First, local invertibility does not imply that the EOS is globally one-to-one. Symmetries can make different densities produce the same measured observables, or force the local response to vanish for particular states. Reconstruction can then require additional observables or independent input to select an EOS branch, as discussed in Sec. VI . Second, successful readout requires the measured observables to follow the calibrated EOS at the instantaneous local densities. Local equilibration can establish this relation before transport erases the spatial profile, providing a time window for its reconstruction [ 43 , 29 , 33 , 37 , 56 ] . The initial state need not be thermal, and the evolving local state need not be fully described by the Gibbs ensemble. Also, additional conserved quantities can produce deviations from a Gibbs EOS, whose effect on the readout must be assessed explicitly in the case of integrable models, as done in Sec. IV . To quantify reconstruction errors, we write the measured snapshot averages at the true local density 𝒒 \bm{q} as 𝑶 ^ = 𝑶 eq ​ ( 𝒒 ) + 𝒓 + 𝜼 \widehat{\bm{O}}=\bm{O}_{\rm eq}(\bm{q})+\bm{r}+\bm{\eta} , where 𝒓 \bm{r} describes departures from the equilibrium EOS and 𝜼 \bm{\eta} is the fluctuation due to a finite number of samples. The calibrated EOS may also differ from the exact equilibrium relation: 𝑶 cal = 𝑶 eq + δ ​ 𝑶 cal \bm{O}_{\rm cal}=\bm{O}_{\rm eq}+\delta\bm{O}_{\rm cal} . The reconstructed density 𝒒 snap \bm{q}_{\rm snap} is obtained by matching this calibrated relation to the measured averages, 𝑶 cal ​ ( 𝒒 snap ) = 𝑶 ^ \bm{O}_{\rm cal}(\bm{q}_{\rm snap})=\widehat{\bm{O}} . For a square, invertible Jacobian, expanding this equation about the true density 𝒒 \bm{q} gives, to leading order in the errors, 𝒒 snap − 𝒒 ≃ 𝒥 ​ ( 𝒒 ) − 1 ​ ( 𝒓 + 𝜼 − δ ​ 𝑶 cal ​ ( 𝒒 ) ) . \bm{q}_{\rm snap}-\bm{q}\simeq\mathcal{J}(\bm{q})^{-1}\left(\bm{r}+\bm{\eta}-\delta\bm{O}_{\rm cal}(\bm{q})\right). (4) Departures from the EOS and calibration errors therefore produce a systematic shift in the reconstructed density, while sampling fluctuations produce statistical uncertainty. The inverse Jacobian determines how these observable errors translate into density errors. If the observables respond only weakly to density changes, even small observable errors can produce large reconstruction errors. Thus, as in ordinary thermometry, local invertibility alone does not ensure accurate readout. For a single conserved density reconstructed from one observable, averaging over N shot N_{\rm shot} independent snapshots reduces the variance of the measured average by a factor of N shot N_{\rm shot} . The local EOS slope converts this observable uncertainty into density uncertainty, giving Var ⁡ ( q snap ) ≃ Var ⁡ ( O ( 1 ) ) N shot ​ [ O eq ′ ​ ( q ) ] 2 , \operatorname{Var}(q_{\rm snap})\simeq\frac{\operatorname{Var}(O^{(1)})}{N_{\rm shot}[O^{\prime}_{\rm eq}(q)]^{2}}, (5) where O ( 1 ) O^{(1)} is the observable’s value in one snapshot and the derivative is evaluated at the true density q q . Reconstruction is therefore more precise when single-snapshot fluctuations are smaller or the EOS responds more strongly to changes in density [ 12 ] . At fixed nonzero EOS slope and single-snapshot variance, resolving a density contrast Δ ​ q \Delta q with the same relative statistical uncertainty requires N shot ∝ ( Δ ​ q ) − 2 N_{\rm shot}\propto(\Delta q)^{-2} . Increasing the snapshot count reduces this statistical uncertainty but does not remove the systematic error in Eq. ( 4 ), which must also remain small compared with Δ ​ q \Delta q . Finally, at a point where the EOS slope vanishes, Eq. ( 5 ) no longer applies. If the EOS can still be inverted on a selected branch, one can instead obtain a density uncertainty interval by applying that branch’s full inverse EOS to the uncertainty interval of the measured observable. sections.heading: III Energy diffusion
sections.text: As our first example, we will demonstrate the reconstruction of energy spreading in the 1D mixed-field Ising model (MFIM): H ^ MFIM = J ​ ∑ i σ ^ i z ​ σ ^ i + 1 z + g x ​ ∑ i σ ^ i x + g z ​ ∑ i σ ^ i z , \hat{H}_{\rm MFIM}=J\sum_{i}\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{z}\hat{\sigma}_{i+1}^{z}+g_{x}\sum_{i}\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{x}+g_{z}\sum_{i}\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{z}, (6) where σ ^ i x , z \hat{\sigma}_{i}^{x,z} are the standard Pauli matrices. We fix the Ising coupling J = 1 J=1 and set the field strengths to ( g x , g z ) = ( 1.4 , 0.9045 ) (g_{x},g_{z})=(1.4,0.9045) , which places the model far from its integrable limit [ 71 ] . For the Hamiltonian ( 6 ), energy is the only conserved density and spreads diffusively at late times [ 34 , 69 , 71 ] . The local energy h ^ i \hat{h}_{i} in the bulk is h ^ i = J ​ σ ^ i z ​ σ ^ i + 1 z + g x 2 ​ ( σ ^ i x + σ ^ i + 1 x ) + g z 2 ​ ( σ ^ i z + σ ^ i + 1 z ) , \hat{h}_{i}=J\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{z}\hat{\sigma}_{i+1}^{z}+\frac{g_{x}}{2}(\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{x}+\hat{\sigma}_{i+1}^{x})+\frac{g_{z}}{2}(\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{z}+\hat{\sigma}_{i+1}^{z}), (7) where we have divided each local field equally between adjacent bonds. The energy profile to be reconstructed is e i ​ ( t ) = ⟨ h ^ i ⟩ e_{i}(t)=\langle\hat{h}_{i}\rangle , which is clearly not diagonal in the computational basis. Initially, we prepare a thermal domain wall between two Gibbs ensembles, ρ ^ 0 = ρ ^ L ⊗ ρ ^ R , ρ ^ α ∝ e − β α ​ H ^ α , α = L , R , \hat{\rho}_{0}=\hat{\rho}_{L}\otimes\hat{\rho}_{R},\qquad\hat{\rho}_{\alpha}\propto e^{-\beta_{\alpha}\hat{H}_{\alpha}},\quad\alpha=L,R, (8) where H ^ L \hat{H}_{L} and H ^ R \hat{H}_{R} act on the disconnected halves of the chain, see Appendix A for details. The inverse temperatures are set according to β L , R = ∓ δ ​ β \beta_{L,R}=\mp\delta\beta , so that the wall probes energy transport about infinite temperature. Although the reservoirs are initially thermal, the junction is locally out of equilibrium with respect to the full Hamiltonian. To simulate transport efficiently, tensor-network methods such as density matrix truncation (DMT) [ 69 , 71 ] and dissipation-assisted operator evolution (DAOE) [ 53 , 65 , 57 ] retain local information while suppressing the growth of operator entanglement. Here we evolve the state in Eq. ( 8 ) under H ^ MFIM \hat{H}_{\rm MFIM} using DMT, representing the density matrix as a matrix product operator. During bond-dimension compression, DMT preserves the expectation values of short-range operators, including local magnetization and energy density. The transverse-field contribution to the energy cannot be read directly from σ z \sigma^{z} -basis snapshots. The calibrated curve is monotonic over the energy range explored by the wall (see Appendix A ), allowing the magnetization to determine the energy uniquely. sections.heading: IV Reading out multiple conserved densities
sections.text: In the MFIM, magnetization served as an energy thermometer. We now show how to read out energy alongside a conserved magnetization, using two observables extracted from the same snapshots. We consider the spin- 1 / 2 1/2 XXZ chain, H ^ XXZ = ∑ i ( σ ^ i x ​ σ ^ i + 1 x + σ ^ i y ​ σ ^ i + 1 y + Δ ​ σ ^ i z ​ σ ^ i + 1 z ) , \hat{H}_{\mathrm{XXZ}}=\sum_{i}\bigl(\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{x}\hat{\sigma}_{i+1}^{x}+\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{y}\hat{\sigma}_{i+1}^{y}+\Delta\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{z}\hat{\sigma}_{i+1}^{z}\bigr), (12) with anisotropy Δ \Delta . The XXZ model conserves total magnetization, M ^ = 1 2 ​ ∑ i σ ^ i z \hat{M}=\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{z} . While the precise value of anisotropy is unimportant, below we will focus on Δ = 1.5 \Delta=1.5 , where we expect a clear difference between spin and energy transport: at half filling and near infinite temperature, spin transport is diffusive while energy transport is ballistic [ 74 , 35 , 42 ] . We join two Gibbs reservoirs as in Eq. ( 8 ), now with ρ ^ α ∝ e − β α ​ H ^ α − μ α ​ M ^ α , α = L , R , \hat{\rho}_{\alpha}\propto e^{-\beta_{\alpha}\hat{H}_{\alpha}-\mu_{\alpha}\hat{M}_{\alpha}},\quad\alpha=L,R, (13) with β L , R = ∓ δ ​ β \beta_{L,R}=\mp\delta\beta and μ L , R = ∓ δ ​ μ \mu_{L,R}=\mp\delta\mu . The same σ z \sigma^{z} -basis snapshots give the magnetization m i = ⟨ σ ^ i z ⟩ m_{i}=\langle\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{z}\rangle and nearest-neighbor correlation C i = ⟨ σ ^ i z ​ σ ^ i + 1 z ⟩ C_{i}=\langle\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{z}\hat{\sigma}_{i+1}^{z}\rangle . Within the uniform Gibbs family, these observables satisfy C = C eq ​ ( e , m ) C=C_{\rm eq}(e,m) . At half filling and near infinite temperature, the inverse relation gives the energy per bond as e eq ​ ( m , C ) = 2 + Δ 2 Δ ​ C − 2 Δ ​ m 2 + O ⁡ ( C 2 , C ​ m 2 , m 4 ) , e_{\rm eq}(m,C)=\frac{2+\Delta^{2}}{\Delta}C-\frac{2}{\Delta}m^{2}+O(C^{2},Cm^{2},m^{4}), (14) which is derived in Appendix B . One may be tempted to use the linear term for energy readout, e lin = ( ( 2 + Δ 2 ) / Δ ) ​ C e_{\rm lin}=((2+\Delta^{2})/\Delta)C . At finite magnetization, however, the m 2 m^{2} correction matters; e.g., at β = 0 \beta=0 the Gibbs state factorizes, giving C = m 2 C=m^{2} and e = Δ ​ m 2 e=\Delta m^{2} , so the linear readout overestimates the energy by 2 ​ m 2 / Δ 2m^{2}/\Delta . Figure 3 (a) compares the reconstructed against the directly computed energy profiles at the finite steps δ ​ β = 0.01 \delta\beta=0.01 and δ ​ μ = 0.1 \delta\mu=0.1 . For reconstruction, we use the full numerical EOS, calibrated independently in uniform L = 128 L=128 Gibbs-MPO states, and invert it at the measured magnetization: e snap ​ ( x , t ) = e eq ​ ( m ⁡ ( x , t ) , C ⁡ ( x , t ) ) . e_{\rm snap}(x,t)=e_{\rm eq}\!\bigl(m(x,t),C(x,t)\bigr). (15) We see that the joint EOS removes the offset of the linear readout and closely reproduces the evolving energy front. Figure 3 (b)-(c) shows that the magnetization spreads approximately diffusively near the junction, while the reconstructed energy spreads ballistically. To compare their spreading more quantitatively, we define an effective transfer length within symmetric spatial windows on either side of the junction, ℓ q ​ ( t ) = ∑ i > 0 δ ​ q i ​ ( t ) − ∑ i < 0 δ ​ q i ​ ( t ) q L − q R , q = m ​ or ​ e snap , \ell_{q}(t)=\frac{\sum_{i>0}\delta q_{i}(t)-\sum_{i<0}\delta q_{i}(t)}{q_{L}-q_{R}},\quad q=m\;\text{or}\;e_{\rm snap}, (16) where δ ​ q i ​ ( t ) ≡ q i ​ ( t ) − q i ​ ( 0 ) \delta q_{i}(t)\equiv q_{i}(t)-q_{i}(0) and q L , R q_{L,R} are the initial reservoir values. The numerator adds the density gained on the right to that lost on the left. Dividing by the initial density contrast expresses this redistribution as a length in chain units, allowing spin and energy transport to be compared on the same footing. For a profile that broadens with a fixed scaling shape, ℓ q ​ ( t ) \ell_{q}(t) is proportional to the width of the spreading region. Figure 3 (d) shows ℓ m ​ ( t ) \ell_{m}(t) and ℓ e snap ​ ( t ) \ell_{e_{\rm snap}}(t) growing approximately as t 1 / 2 t^{1/2} and t t , respectively, before boundary effects set in. The snapshot estimates closely follow the curves obtained from expectation values, resolving the different spreading laws from the same set of measurement data. Unlike the MFIM example considered in Sec. III , the 1D spin- 1 / 2 1/2 XXZ chain is integrable and the additional conserved quantities can cause departures from the Gibbs EOS [ 25 , 3 ] . For a purely thermal weak wall at Δ = 1.5 \Delta=1.5 , linearized generalized hydrodynamics [ 9 , 3 ] bounds the energy readout error by approximately 4.7 % 4.7\% of the full reservoir energy contrast, see Appendix B for the derivation and numerical checks. The XXZ chain nevertheless provides a particularly clear demonstration of simultaneous readout of distinct transport laws. To establish that the joint-readout principle does not rely on integrability, we additionally demonstrate its application to the nonintegrable spin- 1 1 Heisenberg chain in Appendix C .

sections.heading: V Floquet readout with off-diagonal charge
sections.text: Local equilibrium relations also enable readout of conserved charges in periodically driven systems or quantum circuits without energy conservation [ 15 , 31 , 52 ] . Below we illustrate this on a spin- 1 1 Floquet circuit that conserves N ^ = ∑ j n ^ j \hat{N}=\sum_{j}\hat{n}_{j} , with the charge operator defined as n ^ j = ( S ^ j x ) 2 \hat{n}_{j}=(\hat{S}_{j}^{x})^{2} . This operator is not diagonal in the S z S^{z} measurement basis, but local relaxation makes it accessible through the EOS. We demonstrate this using two nonthermal preparations with different charge profiles but identical initial snapshot distributions. First, we explain the circuit construction. We will work in the orthonormal local basis, | 0 x ⟩ = ( | + 1 z ⟩ − | − 1 z ⟩ ) / 2 |0_{x}\rangle=(|+1_{z}\rangle-|-1_{z}\rangle)/\sqrt{2} , | 0 y ⟩ = ( | + 1 z ⟩ + | − 1 z ⟩ ) / 2 |0_{y}\rangle=(|+1_{z}\rangle+|-1_{z}\rangle)/\sqrt{2} , | 0 z ⟩ = | S z = 0 ⟩ |0_{z}\rangle=|S^{z}=0\rangle , in which the charge operator is diagonal, n ^ = diag ⁡ ( 0 , 1 , 1 ) \hat{n}=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,1) . sections.heading: VI Symmetry constraints and branch-resolved reconstruction
sections.text: Symmetries can make equilibrium readout globally ambiguous even after local equilibration. We illustrate this limitation in the kinetically constrained PXP model [ 19 , 38 ] , which describes resonantly driven Rydberg atom chains in the nearest-neighbor blockade limit [ 7 , 2 , 6 , 73 ] (the same model can also be realized in a tilted Bose-Hubbard optical lattice [ 58 ] ). In this case, the site-resolved measurements of atomic state occupations provide the Z Z -basis snapshots considered below. The PXP Hamiltonian is H ^ = ∑ i P ^ i − 1 ​ X ^ i ​ P ^ i + 1 , P ^ i = 1 + Z ^ i 2 , \hat{H}=\sum_{i}\hat{P}_{i-1}\hat{X}_{i}\hat{P}_{i+1},\qquad\hat{P}_{i}=\frac{1+\hat{Z}_{i}}{2}, (24) where X ^ i , Z ^ i \hat{X}_{i},\hat{Z}_{i} are Pauli operators and P ^ i \hat{P}_{i} projects onto the atomic ground state. This projector encodes a kinetic constraint: each atom can be excited only if its nearest neighbors are both in the ground state. The constraint makes the model nonintegrable, giving rise to much interesting physics including quantum many-body scars [ 63 , 21 , 39 , 24 , 10 , 32 , 59 , 49 , 30 ] and superdiffusive energy transport [ 41 , 5 , 26 ] . Here we test equilibrium readout during the relaxation of an energy wall, Fig. 5 (a). The local energy e i = ⟨ P ^ i − 1 ​ X ^ i ​ P ^ i + 1 ⟩ e_{i}=\langle\hat{P}_{i-1}\hat{X}_{i}\hat{P}_{i+1}\rangle is off-diagonal in the measurement basis, whereas the magnetization m i = ⟨ Z ^ i ⟩ m_{i}=\langle\hat{Z}_{i}\rangle is directly accessible. The PXP model has a “particle-hole” symmetry Γ ^ ​ H ^ ​ Γ ^ = − H ^ \hat{\Gamma}\hat{H}\hat{\Gamma}=-\hat{H} , generated by Γ ^ = ∏ i Z ^ i \hat{\Gamma}=\prod_{i}\hat{Z}_{i} [ 62 , 55 ] . The Gibbs states at opposite inverse temperatures therefore obey ρ ^ − β = Γ ^ ​ ρ ^ β ​ Γ ^ \hat{\rho}_{-\beta}=\hat{\Gamma}\hat{\rho}_{\beta}\hat{\Gamma} . Since Γ ^ \hat{\Gamma} is diagonal in the measurement basis, their snapshot distributions coincide: p − β ​ ( 𝐬 ) = ⟨ 𝐬 | ρ ^ − β | 𝐬 ⟩ = ⟨ 𝐬 | ρ ^ β | 𝐬 ⟩ = p β ​ ( 𝐬 ) . p_{-\beta}(\mathbf{s})=\langle\mathbf{s}|\hat{\rho}_{-\beta}|\mathbf{s}\rangle=\langle\mathbf{s}|\hat{\rho}_{\beta}|\mathbf{s}\rangle=p_{\beta}(\mathbf{s}). (25) These states have opposite energies, so the energy sign cannot be determined even with arbitrarily many snapshots and access to all diagonal correlations. In particular, the magnetization EOS is even: m eq ​ ( − e ) = m eq ​ ( e ) . m_{\rm eq}(-e)=m_{\rm eq}(e). (26) Its two branches therefore give the same measured magnetization, as illustrated in Fig. 5 (a). However, independent information about the spatial profile can select the appropriate branch. Let g ​ ( e ) = m eq ​ ( e ) g(e)=m_{\rm eq}(e) denote the positive-energy branch, monotonic over the calibrated interval. Local equilibrium gives m ⁡ ( x , t ) ≃ g ⁡ ( | e ⁡ ( x , t ) | ) m(x,t)\simeq g(|e(x,t)|) , allowing the measured magnetization to determine the energy magnitude. For the wall considered here, the preparation fixes negative energy on the left and positive energy on the right [Fig. 5 (a)]. Provided that the evolving profile retains a single zero crossing at the wall center x = 0 x=0 , this information determines the sign: e rec ​ ( x , t ) = sgn ⁡ ( x ) ​ g − 1 ​ [ m ⁡ ( x , t ) ] . e_{\rm rec}(x,t)=\operatorname{sgn}(x)\,g^{-1}\!\left[m(x,t)\right]. (27) The EOS thus supplies the magnitude, while the wall orientation and assumed zero-crossing structure supply the EOS branch, see Fig. 5 (a). With the knowledge of the branch structure of the EOS, we can perform energy reconstruction during the wall’s evolution, summarized in Fig. 5 (b)-(c). The EOS of the PXP model is calibrated independently in uniform Gibbs states on a small chain of L = 16 L=16 atoms with periodic boundary conditions. At later times, the reconstructed energy follows the directly computed profile over much of the calibrated range, although local deviations remain. Magnetization values outside that range have no inverse under the calibrated EOS and are excluded, as indicated by the red crosses. We note that the EOS, being an even function of e e , also has a vanishing slope at e = 0 e=0 , making inversion poorly conditioned near the junction. Small departures from the EOS or finite-sampling fluctuations can therefore produce comparatively large energy errors, as discussed in Sec. II . The PXP example thus illustrates two distinct aspects of the readout: prior spatial information enables reconstruction from a globally ambiguous EOS, while local EOS sensitivity controls error amplification.

sections.heading: VIII Conclusions
sections.text: We have shown how local equilibration and an independently calibrated EOS enable reconstruction of conserved-density profiles from fixed-basis snapshots, even when the corresponding operators contain off-diagonal terms. Our numerical examples recover energy fronts and a diffusion constant, distinguish diffusive spin transport from ballistic energy spreading, and reveal hidden conserved-charge profiles in a Floquet system. We quantify how weak EOS responses and departures from Gibbs equilibrium affect the readout, and show how prior information about the preparation and spatial structure can resolve symmetry-imposed ambiguities. We also relate PCA entropy to the local spin variance, clarifying when it can serve as a transport diagnostic. These results establish snapshot thermometry as a quantitative probe of transport beyond scaling exponents. Looking ahead, snapshot thermometry could broaden the range of conserved quantities accessible from existing snapshot measurements in experiments on Rydberg atom arrays [ 2 , 11 ] , optical lattices [ 68 ] , trapped ions [ 27 ] , and superconducting qubits [ 16 ] . In such applications, the readout should be tailored to the measurement capabilities of each platform. The EOS response and snapshot fluctuations provide quantitative criteria for selecting observables that maximize reconstruction precision at a fixed sampling budget, offering a route towards systematic, experiment-specific optimization. On the theoretical side, a natural extension is to develop calibrations based on generalized Gibbs ensembles or equilibrium within dynamically accessible sectors, where conventional Gibbs relations may be insufficient [ 25 , 73 ] . The coupling of nonconserved observables to conserved densities and their products connects this readout mechanism to hierarchical relaxation [ 66 ] and hydrodynamic descriptions of higher-order correlators [ 67 , 46 ] . These connections motivate extending snapshot thermometry from mean density profiles to fluctuations and spatial correlations of transported quantities, with the prospect of testing dynamical universality through higher-order cumulants [ 16 ] . We show how local equilibration and an independently calibrated equilibrium equation of state can reveal otherwise hidden conserved-density profiles. We demonstrate numerically that such “quantum snapshot thermometry” can recover energy fronts and a diffusion constant, distinguish spin transport from energy spreading, and reveal conserved-charge profiles invisible in the initial measurements. We also identify symmetry-imposed ambiguities in the readout and show how prior knowledge of the spatial structure can resolve them. Fixed-basis snapshot thermometry thus provides quantitative hydrodynamic information beyond transport exponents, bypassing additional measurement bases and quantum state tomography. This reconstruction requires a sufficient set of observables with independent responses to the conserved densities. I Introduction In analog quantum simulators, key information about the many-body wave function is extracted from site-resolved projective measurements [ 1 , 2 , 68 , 27 , 16 ] . These wave-function snapshots give direct access to observables that are diagonal in the measurement basis. However, many quantities of interest, such as local energy, contain off-diagonal terms and thus cannot be directly determined from the snapshots. Such observables can be accessed through additional measurement settings, including basis rotations and randomized measurement protocols [ 23 , 18 ] , which can be challenging on platforms with limited coherent control [ 40 ] . Alternatively, off-diagonal observables can be inferred from fixed-basis measurements following known Hamiltonian dynamics [ 22 , 40 , 51 ] , although reconstructing them can require computationally expensive processing in an exponentially large Hilbert space. Hamiltonian shadow protocols alleviate this cost by using independently evolving patches [ 40 ] , while other protocols employ ancillary degrees of freedom [ 61 , 44 ] . These approaches use dedicated quantum dynamics to encode information into measurement outcomes, motivating a complementary strategy that exploits local equilibration during the dynamics of interest. Recent work has proposed that principal component analysis (PCA) of wave-function snapshots can diagnose transport and extract the associated dynamical exponents [ 4 , 70 ] . The observed correspondence between PCA entropy and energy transport raises the question of how a conserved-density profile becomes encoded in snapshot statistics when the corresponding operator is not diagonal in the measurement basis. Understanding this mechanism could enable quantitative reconstruction of the evolving profile, including its amplitude and shape, beyond transport exponents. A possible route is suggested by equilibrium thermometry, where equations of state and fluctuation relations connect measurable observables to thermodynamic quantities [ 47 , 36 , 20 , 50 ] . Atom-resolved fluctuation measurements have also enabled local thermometry without requiring global thermal equilibrium [ 13 ] . Here we show that local equilibration enables quantitative reconstruction of hidden conserved-density profiles from fixed-basis snapshots, without additional measurement operations or global dynamical reconstruction. Once local equilibration is established, an independently calibrated equilibrium equation of state (EOS) relates measurable diagonal observables to the local conserved densities. Where this relation is locally invertible, it converts snapshot averages into the density profile [Fig. 1 (a)]. Note that global invertibility is not essential: independent information about the preparation and spatial structure of the evolving profile can select the appropriate EOS branch. We demonstrate that this readout recovers the shape and amplitude of energy fronts and enables extraction of the diffusion constant. With multiple conserved quantities, different observables extracted from the same snapshots distinguish their transport responses, e.g., spin transport from energy spreading [Fig. 1 (b)]. The framework also applies beyond energy-conserving dynamics, enabling reconstruction of conserved-charge profiles in Floquet circuits that are not directly accessible in the measurement basis. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the local-equilibrium readout, its requirements and sources of error. Sections III - V apply this approach to numerically demonstrate energy reconstruction in the mixed-field Ising model, joint spin and energy readout in the XXZ chain, and hidden conserved-charge reconstruction in a Floquet circuit, respectively. Section VI examines symmetry-imposed ambiguities and branch-resolved reconstruction on the example of blockaded Rydberg atom arrays. Section VII explains the relation of PCA entropy [ 4 , 70 ] with local spin variance and identifies conditions under which it inherits transport scaling. Our conclusions are presented in Section VIII , while the appendices provide supporting analytical and numerical details. II Local equilibration and readout Let 𝒒 ⁡ ( x , t ) ≡ { q a ​ ( x , t ) } \bm{q}(x,t)\equiv\{q_{a}(x,t)\} denote a set of local conserved densities, while 𝑶 ⁡ ( x , t ) ≡ { O a ​ ( x , t ) } \bm{O}(x,t)\equiv\{O_{a}(x,t)\} are the diagonal observables accessible from snapshots. Local equilibration relates these observables to the conserved densities through an equilibrium equation of state (EOS) [ 54 ] : O a ​ ( x , t ) = O a , eq ​ [ 𝒒 ⁡ ( x , t ) ] + r a ​ ( x , t ) , O_{a}(x,t)=O_{a,\mathrm{eq}}[\bm{q}(x,t)]+r_{a}(x,t), (1) where r a r_{a} denotes departures from the chosen equilibrium relation, including the influence of possible degrees of freedom beyond 𝒒 \bm{q} . For the example in Fig. 1 (a) with a single conserved density, r a r_{a} is the vertical displacement from the equilibrium curve at a given density q q , and the orange arrow depicts the process of local relaxation toward this curve. Once r a r_{a} becomes small, the measured average O meas O_{\rm meas} gives the reconstructed density q snap = O eq − 1 ​ ( O meas ) , q_{\rm snap}=O_{\rm eq}^{-1}(O_{\rm meas}), (2) on a selected invertible EOS branch. This forms the basis of our thermometry protocol, illustrated by dashed arrows in Fig. 1 (a). The described protocol requires knowledge of 𝑶 eq ​ ( 𝒒 ) \bm{O}_{\rm eq}(\bm{q}) , which should be obtained via an independent calibration. We do this by evaluating the diagonal observables and conserved densities in uniform equilibrium states spanning the relevant density range. In this work, we will focus on one-dimensional (1D) systems and finite-temperature regimes, where local equilibrium averages can be evaluated efficiently using thermal matrix product state (MPS) methods, with the system size needed for calibration set by convergence of the local observables. However, the thermometry protocol itself is not dimension-specific. In higher dimensions, the EOS could be obtained using other numerical methods or experimental measurements, provided that they associate observable values with independently determined conserved densities. At fixed system parameters, the same EOS can be reused for different preparations whenever the evolving observables follow the calibrated relation. For small deviations from a uniform reference density 𝒒 0 \bm{q}_{0} , the linear response is governed by the EOS Jacobian 𝒥 a ​ α ​ ( 𝒒 ) = ∂ O a , eq ​ ( 𝒒 ) ∂ q α , \mathcal{J}_{a\alpha}(\bm{q})=\frac{\partial O_{a,\mathrm{eq}}(\bm{q})}{\partial q_{\alpha}}, (3) evaluated at 𝒒 = 𝒒 0 \bm{q}=\bm{q}_{0} . For a single conserved quantity, a nonzero EOS slope allows readout from one diagonal observable. For energy readout, this derivative also characterizes the observable’s leading coupling to the slow energy mode, connecting the EOS response to hydrodynamic relaxation [ 8 , 67 ] . With several conserved quantities, each observable generally mixes their contributions. Resolving all densities q a q_{a} at linear order requires 𝒥 \mathcal{J} to have full column rank, so that the observables respond independently to changes in the densities. For equal numbers of observables and densities, this condition reduces to det 𝒥 ≠ 0 \det\mathcal{J}\neq 0 . Furthermore, when linearization about 𝒒 0 \bm{q}_{0} is insufficient, reconstruction should use the full EOS. Figure 1 (b) illustrates the general protocol with multiple hidden conserved densities q a q_{a} reconstructed from diagonal observables O a O_{a} , measured in the same ensemble of snapshots. A typical example is the joint readout of spin and energy: while magnetization m m is diagonal in the standard Pauli basis, energy e e contains off-diagonal terms that ordinarily require additional measurement settings to access. The same snapshot ensemble provides the local magnetization m i = ⟨ σ ^ i z ⟩ m_{i}=\langle\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{z}\rangle and nearest-neighbor correlation C i = ⟨ σ ^ i z ​ σ ^ i + 1 z ⟩ C_{i}=\langle\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{z}\hat{\sigma}_{i+1}^{z}\rangle . In the notation above, these correspond to 𝒒 = ( m , e ) \bm{q}=(m,e) and 𝑶 = ( m , C ) \bm{O}=(m,C) . Magnetization gives the spin density m ⁡ ( x , t ) m(x,t) directly. The independently calibrated relation C = C eq ​ ( e , m ) C=C_{\rm eq}(e,m) then determines the energy e ⁡ ( x , t ) e(x,t) from the measured magnetization, provided that ∂ e C eq ≠ 0 \partial_{e}C_{\rm eq}\neq 0 . A few comments are in order. First, local invertibility does not imply that the EOS is globally one-to-one. Symmetries can make different densities produce the same measured observables, or force the local response to vanish for particular states. Reconstruction can then require additional observables or independent input to select an EOS branch, as discussed in Sec. VI . Second, successful readout requires the measured observables to follow the calibrated EOS at the instantaneous local densities. Local equilibration can establish this relation before transport erases the spatial profile, providing a time window for its reconstruction [ 43 , 29 , 33 , 37 , 56 ] . The initial state need not be thermal, and the evolving local state need not be fully described by the Gibbs ensemble. Also, additional conserved quantities can produce deviations from a Gibbs EOS, whose effect on the readout must be assessed explicitly in the case of integrable models, as done in Sec. IV . To quantify reconstruction errors, we write the measured snapshot averages at the true local density 𝒒 \bm{q} as 𝑶 ^ = 𝑶 eq ​ ( 𝒒 ) + 𝒓 + 𝜼 \widehat{\bm{O}}=\bm{O}_{\rm eq}(\bm{q})+\bm{r}+\bm{\eta} , where 𝒓 \bm{r} describes departures from the equilibrium EOS and 𝜼 \bm{\eta} is the fluctuation due to a finite number of samples. The calibrated EOS may also differ from the exact equilibrium relation: 𝑶 cal = 𝑶 eq + δ ​ 𝑶 cal \bm{O}_{\rm cal}=\bm{O}_{\rm eq}+\delta\bm{O}_{\rm cal} . The reconstructed density 𝒒 snap \bm{q}_{\rm snap} is obtained by matching this calibrated relation to the measured averages, 𝑶 cal ​ ( 𝒒 snap ) = 𝑶 ^ \bm{O}_{\rm cal}(\bm{q}_{\rm snap})=\widehat{\bm{O}} . For a square, invertible Jacobian, expanding this equation about the true density 𝒒 \bm{q} gives, to leading order in the errors, 𝒒 snap − 𝒒 ≃ 𝒥 ​ ( 𝒒 ) − 1 ​ ( 𝒓 + 𝜼 − δ ​ 𝑶 cal ​ ( 𝒒 ) ) . \bm{q}_{\rm snap}-\bm{q}\simeq\mathcal{J}(\bm{q})^{-1}\left(\bm{r}+\bm{\eta}-\delta\bm{O}_{\rm cal}(\bm{q})\right). (4) Departures from the EOS and calibration errors therefore produce a systematic shift in the reconstructed density, while sampling fluctuations produce statistical uncertainty. The inverse Jacobian determines how these observable errors translate into density errors. If the observables respond only weakly to density changes, even small observable errors can produce large reconstruction errors. Thus, as in ordinary thermometry, local invertibility alone does not ensure accurate readout. For a single conserved density reconstructed from one observable, averaging over N shot N_{\rm shot} independent snapshots reduces the variance of the measured average by a factor of N shot N_{\rm shot} . The local EOS slope converts this observable uncertainty into density uncertainty, giving Var ⁡ ( q snap ) ≃ Var ⁡ ( O ( 1 ) ) N shot ​ [ O eq ′ ​ ( q ) ] 2 , \operatorname{Var}(q_{\rm snap})\simeq\frac{\operatorname{Var}(O^{(1)})}{N_{\rm shot}[O^{\prime}_{\rm eq}(q)]^{2}}, (5) where O ( 1 ) O^{(1)} is the observable’s value in one snapshot and the derivative is evaluated at the true density q q . Reconstruction is therefore more precise when single-snapshot fluctuations are smaller or the EOS responds more strongly to changes in density [ 12 ] . At fixed nonzero EOS slope and single-snapshot variance, resolving a density contrast Δ ​ q \Delta q with the same relative statistical uncertainty requires N shot ∝ ( Δ ​ q ) − 2 N_{\rm shot}\propto(\Delta q)^{-2} . Increasing the snapshot count reduces this statistical uncertainty but does not remove the systematic error in Eq. ( 4 ), which must also remain small compared with Δ ​ q \Delta q . Finally, at a point where the EOS slope vanishes, Eq. ( 5 ) no longer applies. If the EOS can still be inverted on a selected branch, one can instead obtain a density uncertainty interval by applying that branch’s full inverse EOS to the uncertainty interval of the measured observable. VI Symmetry constraints and branch-resolved reconstruction Symmetries can make equilibrium readout globally ambiguous even after local equilibration. We illustrate this limitation in the kinetically constrained PXP model [ 19 , 38 ] , which describes resonantly driven Rydberg atom chains in the nearest-neighbor blockade limit [ 7 , 2 , 6 , 73 ] (the same model can also be realized in a tilted Bose-Hubbard optical lattice [ 58 ] ). In this case, the site-resolved measurements of atomic state occupations provide the Z Z -basis snapshots considered below. The PXP Hamiltonian is H ^ = ∑ i P ^ i − 1 ​ X ^ i ​ P ^ i + 1 , P ^ i = 1 + Z ^ i 2 , \hat{H}=\sum_{i}\hat{P}_{i-1}\hat{X}_{i}\hat{P}_{i+1},\qquad\hat{P}_{i}=\frac{1+\hat{Z}_{i}}{2}, (24) where X ^ i , Z ^ i \hat{X}_{i},\hat{Z}_{i} are Pauli operators and P ^ i \hat{P}_{i} projects onto the atomic ground state.
